newsitem.title: GERMANY: Once taboo, EMU delay option enters German debate.
newsitem.headline: Once taboo, EMU delay option enters German debate.

text.p: Delaying the start of Europe's monetary union, an issue once strictly taboo in Bonn, is now becoming part of Germany's complex debate on how to reconcile a pro-European elite with an anti-EMU electorate.

The view is a minority one, usually aired after phrases like "well, if we can't make the criteria, then..." But the fact it is discussed more openly is notable in a country where until recently few leaders admitted doubts about the project.
Chancellor Helmut Kohl still vehemently supports the 1999 start-up date for the euro. Most business leaders and politicians in both his camp and the opposition agree.
Finance Minister Theo Waigel told journalists on Thursday: "We are in the middle of the year that will decide currency union, so talk of a delay would be wrong."
But the government's failed grab for Bundesbank gold to prop up its 1997 budget to qualify for the single currency seems to have opened the public debate to other options.

Pollsters have started asking Germans whether they would support a delay. With widespread public reluctance to give up the deutschemark, it was no surprise when weekly newspaper Die Woche said on Thursday 71 percent of those it polled backed a delay.

Only 21 percent of the 1,002 people surveyed thought EMU should go ahead on time despite the growing problems seen in meeting the Maastricht criteria according to the strict interpretation the Bundesbank and politicians have put on it.
Talk about a delay arose last weekend when Der Spiegel news magazine quoted Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer as asking whether it would be possible -- a statement the bank promptly denied.

But, as the business daily Handelsblatt wrote on Thursday: "It is hard to escape the impression members of the Bonn coalition have that the Bundesbank and its president want to either delay EMU if not block it."
On Monday, key Waigel ally Alois Glueck, state assembly majority leader for Waigel's Christian Social Union (CSU) in sceptical Bavaria, stressed "stability before speed" in his call for a delay.

The opposition Social Democrats' mildly sceptical star, Lower Saxony state premier Gerhard Schroeder, called for a delay in an interview this week, as did Hans Apel, a former SPD finance minister and now a university economics professor.

Even among Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), some politicians are beginning to say the intense German focus on the three percent deficit-to-GDP is, as young CDU deputy Armin Laschet called it, "a phantom discussion".
He backed a looser interpretation.
Kohl made his point clear once again in parliament on Wednesday when he said he wanted EMU to start on time, saying a delay would cause havoc on financial markets.
"The government has no incentive to even think about a delay until the spring of next year, when the first group of members is named," said Ros Lifton of HSBC Markets in London.
"The last thing you want is the possibility of a D-mark appreciation messing up a recovery."

But CDU officials are not so sure Bonn can hold its hard line that long. "If we reach the autumn and it's clear we will not make the 3.0 percent target, there will have to be some change or we could stand accused of being liars," one said.
CDU strategists have long bet on Kohl's credibility to win out over anti-EMU sentiment, even in an election year like 1998, but this seems to be weakening.
An Electoral Research Group poll showed only 22 percent saw the CDU as the better party on economic issues, compared to 21 percent for the SPD and 31 percent for "none of the above".
In the EMU poll by the Forsa group, only 37 percent thought Germany could actually meet the Maastricht criteria while 45 percent said it could not.
Asked if the Kohl government could solve Germany's economic problems, 71 percent said "no" and only 21 percent said "yes".

Fifty-two percent wanted Waigel to step down and 57 percent said the respected Bundesbank, which forced Bonn to put off its plans for a gold payout this year, should not even revalue its underpriced gold stocks.
